summary: Fothergill saw the boy acting in a Greek play at Bradfield College, bought a photograph of the cast, and wrote to him, giving 30 Manchester Street as his address so that the boy might visit. Two letters came back. A firm of solicitors then required an undertaking that he write no more, on threat of putting the matter before the police; he gave it and heard nothing further.

sources.quote: At a Greek play at Bradfield, I gazed longingly at the charming face of a boy on the stage. I bought a photo of the group with the boy in the middle. Quite infatuated, I dined that night at the old fashioned hotel in Manchester Street and wrote to him on their note paper, and got a couple of nice letters in return. Then, in order to have him visit me I gave No. 30 Manchester Street as my address.
sources.context: Fothergill's memoir, as printed by Sox, who introduces it as a 'silly indiscretion' Fothergill recalled from the period after his return from Berneval
sources.supports: Fothergill's own account of the approach, in his own words.
sources.provenance: PDF p. 158 (printed folio 142 confirmed on the rendered page).

sources.quote: They said, in the end that no man of the world reading my letter (which incidentally had been perfectly nice) could possibly form two opinions about my intentions toward the boy, and that I must undertake not to rewrite to him again, otherwise they must put the matter before the police. I felt a fool and afraid.

sources.supports: How the approach ended, and the legal pressure that ended it - three years after Wilde's release, the same criminal law operating without a prosecution.
